canonical_rules.representative_verbatim: A 51-year-old male known for psoriasis and treated with adalimumab (Humira ® ) since 2002, presented a few asymptomatic papules of the glans penis since 2008. The first biopsy concluded a CA and the patient was treated with cryotherapy, with no significant benefit. During the last physical examination in September 2018, whitish papules of the glans penis were still present (Fig. 1). The differential diagnosis was clinically CA versus intraepithelial neoplasm versus psoriasis. The patient had stopped his treatment of adalimumab 6 months previously and in spite of that, the psoriasis was clinically mild with a PASI score of 2.5. A new biopsy of the penis was performed. Histologically, dysplasia could be excluded. Acanthosis and hyperkeratosis with variable degree of papillomatosis were present (Fig. 2a). The keratinocytes of the granular and spinous layer showed cytoplasmic vacuolization, coarse keratohyaline granules, and eosinophilic inclusions, consistent with EA (Fig. 2b, c). The review of the first biopsy in 2008 diagnosed as CA showed the same histological image and allowed the same conclusion. As the patient did not experience any inconvenience, no further treatment was continued.

findings.verbatim_support: A 51-year-old male known for psoriasis and treated with adalimumab (Humira ® ) since 2002, presented a few asymptomatic papules of the glans penis since 2008. During the last physical examination in September 2018, whitish papules of the glans penis were still present (Fig. 1). findings.claim: Epidermolytic acanthoma (EA) -> acanthosis and hyperkeratosis with variable degree of papillomatosis
findings.verbatim_support: The histopathologic features are acanthosis and hyperkeratosis with variable degree of papillomatosis. Ackerman described EA 50 years ago as a combination of variously sized clear spaces around nuclei in the stratum spinosum and granulosum, amphophilic material forming indistinct cellular boundaries, markedly thickened granular zone containing keratohyalin bodies, and compact hyperkeratosis. This pattern differs from the cytopathogenic effect of HPV, where a clear halo around the nucleus is homogenous and the nucleus is retracted. Acantholysis is also different, as cytoplasm is eosinophilic and the nucleus is hyperchromatic. Four histological patterns of EA have been described, which may coexist in the same lesion. They consist of the papillomatous, cup-shaped, acanthomatous, and polypoid variants. Ultrastructural studies have shown tonofilament alterations with agglutination of them in the cytoplasm and intracellular vacuolization, as well as premature cornification of keratinocytes [2, 7].

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk describes the histopathological, ultrastructural, and differential diagnostic features of Epidermolytic Acanthoma (EA). The key histopathologic features are acanthosis, hyperkeratosis (including compact hyperkeratosis), and variable-degree papillomatosis [S1|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. Ackerman's classic description includes variously sized perinuclear clear spaces in the stratum spinosum and granulosum, amphophilic material forming indistinct cellular boundaries, markedly thickened granular zone with keratohyalin bodies, and compact hyperkeratosis [S2|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. These features are distinguished from HPV koilocytic effect (homogeneous perinuclear halo with retracted nucleus) [S3|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709] and from acantholysis (eosinophilic cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nucleus) [S4|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. Four histological variants — papillomatous, cup-shaped, acanthomatous, and polypoid — have been described and may coexist in the same lesion [S5–S6|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709]. Ultrastructural studies reveal tonofilament agglutination in the cytoplasm, intracellular vacuolization, and premature cornification of keratinocytes [S7|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7709].

map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk addresses the etiology and management of EA (epidermal acanthoma) in relation to HPV and other proposed causes. Molecular studies have consistently failed to detect a viral genome in EA, and p16 immunostaining is uniformly negative in both solitary and multiple lesions [S2|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7712]. Epidemiologically, EA occurs in patients without prior sexually transmitted diseases or risky sexual behavior, further arguing against an HPV-driven etiology [S3|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7712]. Trauma/chronic scratching and immunosuppression have been proposed as alternative etiological factors, though supporting evidence is weak [S4–S5|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7712]. From a treatment perspective, no intervention is required; however, options including surgical excision, cryotherapy, and topical immune modulators are available for cosmetically bothered patients, with variable response rates [S6|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7712].

map_chunks.summary_text: Condyloma acuminatum (CA) is an HPV-induced lesion occurring predominantly on the genitalia of young adults [S1]. Clinically, CA presents as fleshy exophytic lesions, often larger than epidermodysplasia acuminatum (EA), and can involve the glans penis, penile shaft, penile root, pubic area, groin, and perianal area — in contrast to EA, which preferentially affects the scrotum in men and the labia majora in women [S2]. Histologically, CA resembles EA by sharing acanthosis, papillomatosis, and hyperkeratosis [S3], and coarse keratohyalin granules may occasionally be observed [S4]. Key distinguishing histological features of CA include the usual absence of acantholysis and the presence of a homogenous perinuclear halo with a retracted nucleus [S5].

map_chunks.summary_text: This concluding chunk emphasizes the clinical importance of correctly distinguishing EA (eccrine angiomatous hamartoma) from CA (condyloma acuminatum). An incorrect CA diagnosis may cause unnecessary psychosocial anxiety [S1|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7715]. EA is characterized by its usually small size and indolent nature, rendering active treatment unnecessary in most cases [S1|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7715]. Overtreatment can thereby be avoided, with surgical excision reserved only for cosmetic concerns [S2|PMC6827452_dpa-0006-0023|7715].
